newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish investors see government out by 1998.
newsitem.headline: Danish investors see government out by 1998.

text.p: Most Danish institutional investors expect the minority government to lose an election scheduled for 1998 and over 40 percent do not see it surviving the next 12 months, a Danske Invest survey said on Tuesday.

The biannual survey of 51 decision-makers in the country's biggest insurance companies, pension funds, banks and industrial firms showed a sharp drop in the number expecting Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen's centre-left coalition to last its term.
"Six months ago 90 percent expected a general election no earlier than the summer of 1997, now 41 percent expect the government to survive for less than a year," the survey said.
Danske Invest is Denmark's largest investment society, handling over 15 billion crowns for 80,000 members.
Its poll showed that only 10 percent of respondents now expected the Social Democrat-led government to win re-election, compared to 45 percent in its June survey.

Nyrup's government has been the butt of widespread criticism for its handling of a bloody motorcycle gang war and its admittedly bungled attempt to shelve a visit by British author Salman Rushdie, the target of an Iranian death threat.
After failing to reach a compromise with Conservative and Liberal opponents over the 1997 budget the government now depends for its survival on volatile extreme left parties outside the coalition.
A variety of polls show Nyrup's Social Democrats with an approval rating of around 29 percent, their lowest since taking office in 1992
